title: Insomnia test: do I have insomnia? Free sleep self-check — cv.cm
description: Free insomnia test: rate 15 statements about falling asleep, waking at night and how tired you feel during the day over the past month, and see whether it's worth talking to a doctor. Not a diagnosis. Answers stay in your browser.
hint: Thinking about the past month, how well does each statement describe your sleep?
scoreLabel: Insomnia self-check score (0 = few signs, 60 = many)
lede: Do you lie awake for ages, wake up at 3 a.m. or feel wiped out every afternoon? Rate 15 statements about the past month to see how much poor sleep is affecting you, and what can help.
about: Insomnia means having trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early, even when you have the chance to sleep, and feeling the effects during the day: tiredness, low mood, poor concentration or irritability. Almost everyone sleeps badly sometimes. When it happens at least three nights a week for three months or more, doctors call it chronic insomnia; around one adult in ten has it. The most effective treatment is cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), which helps more than sleeping pills in the long run.

The statements here were written for cv.cm around the main signs of insomnia: trouble getting to sleep, waking in the night, waking too early, unrefreshing sleep, worry about sleep and the daytime toll. They are not the Insomnia Severity Index or any other questionnaire, and they haven't been clinically validated, so the score bands are a rough guide, not clinical cut-offs. Loud snoring, gasping in your sleep or an urge to move your legs can point to other sleep problems, so mention them to a doctor. Only a doctor can diagnose insomnia.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree), so the total runs from 0 to 60. 24 or less shows few signs, 25 to 39 some and 40 or more many.

faq.q: How do I know if I have insomnia?
faq.a: If you regularly struggle to fall or stay asleep, or wake too early, at least three nights a week, and it affects how you feel or function during the day, talk to a doctor. This check can help you describe the problem.

Keep the same wake-up time every day, get up if you can't sleep after about 20 minutes, keep the bed for sleep, cut caffeine after midday, and avoid long naps. If it lasts, ask about CBT-I, which works for most people.
Only with a doctor's advice. Sleeping pills can help for a short time, but they can have side effects and don't fix the cause; CBT-I is recommended first.

items: It often takes me more than half an hour to fall asleep.
I wake up during the night and struggle to get back to sleep.
I wake up much earlier than I want to and can't go back to sleep.
I wake up feeling unrefreshed, even after a full night in bed.
I lie in bed with my mind racing.
I worry during the day about whether I'll sleep tonight.
I feel tired or drained most afternoons.
Poor sleep makes it hard for me to concentrate.
I'm more irritable or low because of how I sleep.
My sleep problems happen three or more nights a week.
I often wake more than once a night and lie awake each time.
I need alcohol or sleeping pills to fall asleep.
I feel anxious when it's time to go to bed.
I sleep in or nap a lot to make up for bad nights.
My sleep problems affect my work, study or relationships.

few.name: Few signs of insomnia (0–24)
few.body: Your sleep doesn't seem to be a big problem right now. Everyone has the odd bad night, especially when stressed. Keep the habits that help: a regular wake-up time, daylight in the morning and a calm hour before bed.

some.name: Some signs of insomnia (25–39)
some.body: Poor sleep seems to be affecting you some of the time. Try a steady wake-up time, even at weekends, get up if you can't sleep after about 20 minutes, cut caffeine after midday and keep screens out of bed. If it goes on for weeks or gets worse, talk to a doctor.

many.name: Many signs of insomnia (40–60)
many.body: Your answers show a lot of sleep trouble and its daytime toll. Please talk to a doctor: insomnia is common and treatable, and cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) helps most people. Mention snoring, breathing pauses or restless legs if you have them, as they can point to other sleep problems. If low mood comes with it, the depression check below can help you describe it.
